name: Adelaide Crapsey
credit: Portrait of Adelaide Crapsey (photograph, c. 1900) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Adelaide Crapsey (1878–1914) was an American poet who taught at Smith College and died of tuberculosis at thirty-six.
She devised the cinquain, a five-line form of two, four, six, eight and two syllables, and her only book, Verse, appeared in 1915 after her death.

poems.title: November Night
poems.author: Adelaide Crapsey
poems.text:
Listen ...
With faint dry sound,
Like steps of passing ghosts,
The leaves, frost-crisp’d, break from the trees
And fall.

poems.title: Triad
poems.author: Adelaide Crapsey
poems.text:
These be
Three silent things:
The falling snow ... the hour
Before the dawn ... the mouth of one
Just dead.

poems.title: The Warning
poems.author: Adelaide Crapsey
poems.text:
Just now,
Out of the strange
Still dusk ... as strange, as still ...
A white moth flew. Why am I grown
So cold?

poems.title: On Seeing Weather-Beaten Trees
poems.author: Adelaide Crapsey
poems.text:
Is it as plainly in our living shown,
By slant and twist, which way the wind hath blown?
